name: Bianca Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi, thanks for doing this. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group, not linked to any company, union, party or government. It's all confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I sell flats for Nest & Key, a small agency that does most things online and keeps one little office by the canal. My day starts with the overnight enquiries, which an AI assistant has already sorted into hot, warm and time-wasters. Then I do two or three viewings, maybe a valuation, and in between I'm on my laptop drafting listings and building floor plans from phone scans.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what drains you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the gadget side, honestly, I was the first in the office to use the scanning app and now everyone does. What drains me is the gap between what I sell and what people earn. I sell one-bed flats for more than ten years of a nurse's pay, and I share a flat with two friends because I can't buy one either.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing this?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Six years, since I finished my college diploma in business. I'm decent, not a star. My manager, Femi, says I'm the one who makes the systems work, which is nice but isn't the same as being the best closer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, the tools are handy but they were never going to sell a flat on their own. I'd probably post a little thread about which apps actually earned their keep. The scanning app stays, the chatbot that told a buyer the wrong service charge does not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means I keep my small edge as the person who's good with the tools, and the job stays roughly as it is. My bigger worry is that nothing changes for renters and buyers my age. Housing stays out of reach, including for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools every day and get a bit faster. I'd keep saving, I've got about four months put aside, and I'd look at a shared-ownership flat with my friend Leah in a year or two. And I'd keep going to the housing campaign meetings on Thursdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about work, frustrated about housing. I sell one-bed flats for more than ten years of a nurse's pay, and I can't buy one either. It's a familiar feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your edge is the tools. Doesn't a plateau make that edge smaller?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. If nobody else bothers learning them, I stay a step ahead. If everyone does, I'm just normal, and normal at Nest & Key is still a decent job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Leah about buying together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's do it, but properly, with a written agreement about who owns what. I see couples and friends fall out over flats every month. I'd rather we were boring about it.

say: I'd say the **tools are handy** but were never going to sell a flat alone.
I'd post a thread on which **apps earned their keep** and which didn't.
think: I keep my **small edge** as the person who's good with the tools.
My bigger worry is **housing** staying out of reach for my generation.
do: Keep using the **AI tools daily** and get faster.
Look at a **shared-ownership flat** with Leah within two years.
Keep going to the **housing campaign** meetings on Thursdays.
S0.quote: I sell one-bed flats for more than ten years of a nurse's pay, and I can't buy one either.
fieldNote: Her job feels **secure**; her frustration is with **housing costs**, not AI.
She is openly **proud of the tools** but honest she's average at closing.
Her politics show up as **weekly campaigning**, not just talk.

steps.text: Keep the scanning app and AI enquiry sorting in daily use
Plan a shared-ownership flat with Leah within two years
Keep attending Thursday housing campaign meetings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI's gains should go to people, not just shareholders. Shorter weeks, lower fees for sellers, that sort of thing. I'd also say it's real and people need help learning it, because I've watched colleagues panic about a booking screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm one of the safer ones, because I already run half the systems in our office. But the office itself shrinks. Femi won't replace people who leave, and our admin, Tasha, is doing exactly the tasks on that card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to set up the new tools for the whole team and train people, so the cuts happen to tasks, not people, if I can manage it. I'd ask for a small pay rise for doing that. And I'd teach a couple of free evening sessions for other agents through the campaign group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm okay, mostly, but I'd be watching people I like get squeezed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if training people speeds up the cuts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit that keeps me up. If I make our admin's work quicker, my manager might decide he doesn't need our admin at all. So I'd want it agreed upfront that nobody goes because of what I set up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about leaving estate agency?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. In this picture there's time, and I'd rather be the one shaping how it's used. If it went badly, housing co-ops need people who understand both property and tech.

say: I'd say the gains should go to **people, not shareholders**.
I'd say colleagues need **real help learning** the tools, not just orders.
think: I'm one of the **safer ones** because I already run the office systems.
Our office **shrinks anyway**, and Tasha's work is exactly what the card lists.
do: Set up and **train the team** on the new tools.
Ask Femi for a **pay rise** and a promise nobody is cut for it.
Run **free evening sessions** for other agents through the campaign.
feel: **Uneasy**, mostly okay herself but watching people she likes get squeezed.
S1.quote: If I make our admin's work quicker, my manager might decide he doesn't need our admin at all.
fieldNote: She sees her own job as **fairly safe** but feels guilt about helping cuts along.
She wants a **written promise** from her manager before training others.
Housing co-ops are a **fallback** she brings up unprompted.

steps.text: Set up the new booking system and train all four colleagues
Ask Femi for a raise and a no-cuts promise in writing
Run two free evening AI sessions for local agents

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a moment for big public decisions, like a basic income, and I'd say it loudly. Two years isn't enough for markets to sort it out. I'd be the one at the housing meeting saying jobs and housing are now the same fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my edge with the tools stops mattering. If AI can do any thinking work, it can do mine better than me, and I'm the one who taught it our office's habits. The viewings might hang on till the robots in 2031, but that's not much of a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd apply to housing co-ops and community land trusts, groups that build homes for locals, where the work is meetings and people. I'd keep the savings untouched and drop the shared-ownership plan with Leah for now. I'd use the AI to help me write applications fast, obviously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy. I'd rather be doing something than sitting with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd drop the flat plan. Isn't that a big loss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and it hurts. I'd be twenty-nine with no flat and no career path. A mortgage tied to a job that might vanish is worse than having no flat at twenty-nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you feel you helped bring this on, setting up the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, honestly. Then I remind myself that one agent in one office didn't build any of this. The firms making it, and the governments letting it happen this fast, they own it.

say: I'd push for **big public decisions**, like a basic income.
I'd say **jobs and housing** are now the same fight.
think: My **edge with tools** stops mattering when AI does any thinking work.
The viewings might last until **robots in 2031**, but that's not a career.
do: Apply to **housing co-ops** and community land trusts within months.
Leave the **savings untouched** and drop the shared flat plan for now.
Use **AI to write** job applications quickly.
feel: **Anxious but busy**, preferring action to sitting with the fear.
S2.quote: A mortgage tied to a job that might vanish is worse than having no flat at twenty-nine.
fieldNote: She expects her **own job to go**, but feels in control through quick action.
She feels some **guilt** about setting up tools, then shifts blame to firms and governments.
Housing co-ops are now her **main plan**, not a fallback.

steps.text: Apply to housing co-ops and community land trusts within three months
Drop the shared-ownership flat plan with Leah for now
Keep the four months of savings untouched

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's write the rules now. Who owns these systems, who gets the savings, how people get paid while they retrain. I'd say it at work and online, without shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years feels like enough for me to switch on purpose. I'd be thirty-two. I'd go in with real skills, not as someone who got pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd stay at Nest & Key and get as good as I can at the AI side, then pitch that skill to housing co-ops. I'd do a part-time course in housing development over two years. I'd buy the shared-ownership flat with Leah only if I've moved by year three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but it's a better kind. Five years would feel like the night before an exam, not a fire alarm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year robot gap change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much for me, my job's mostly thinking. It matters for the builders the co-op would hire, though, so I'd want to be part of planning for them too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Femi?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm planning to go in two or three years and I'll help hand everything over. Femi's been good to me. I'd rather leave him a working system than a mess.

say: I'd say use the time to **write the rules** on ownership and savings.
I'd ask how people get **paid while retraining**.
think: Five years is enough to **switch on purpose**, not get pushed.
At thirty-two I'd go into new work with **real skills**.
do: Build up her **AI skills** at Nest & Key for a year.
Study **housing development** part-time over two years.
Buy the **shared flat** with Leah only after moving jobs.
feel: **Anxious**, but like an exam nerve rather than a fire alarm.
S3.quote: Five years would feel like the night before an exam, not a fire alarm.
fieldNote: She still expects her **sales job to end**, so worry stays, but she feels in control.
She plans a **deliberate switch** to housing co-ops by around thirty-two.
Her loyalty to **Femi** shows in her plan to hand over cleanly.

steps.text: Study housing development part-time over two years
Move to a housing co-op role by year three
Buy the shared-ownership flat with Leah after switching jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, if governments actually use it. I'd push for public training and for housing to be part of the plan. And I'd remind everyone that ten years goes fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes me quite hopeful. I'd have time to build a whole second career where people and property meet. I might even do well out of knowing the tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the flat with Leah in the next year or two, because my job looks safe enough for a few years. I'd take on a co-op volunteer role now and start a housing course in year three. By year five I'd move into a co-op or community land trust properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than scared. Mostly it feels like time to plan, which I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy a flat now, in this picture. Why the change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because ten years of a job, even a shrinking one, is enough to get a mortgage going. And if I'm moving into co-op housing work, owning something small gives me a base. I'd still keep it cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything about this picture good for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI goes well, homes could get cheaper to build and sell, which is what I've campaigned on for years. I'd like to be in the room when it happens.

say: I'd say **ten years is plenty** if governments use it well.
I'd push for **public training** and housing in the plan.
think: I feel **quite hopeful** about building a second career.
Knowing the **tech and property** could actually help me.
do: Buy a **cheap shared flat** with Leah within two years.
Take a **co-op volunteer role** now, then a housing course in year three.
Move into **community housing work** by year five.
feel: **Uneasy but hopeful**, more planning than fear.
S4.quote: If AI goes well, homes could get cheaper to build and sell, which is what I've campaigned on for years.
fieldNote: Ten years makes her **hopeful**; she sees a chance to shape housing.
She's still aware her **sales job** won't last, so not fully calm.
The **flat purchase** returns because the job feels safe enough for now.

steps.text: Buy a cheap shared-ownership flat with Leah within two years
Volunteer with a local housing co-op starting this year
Start a housing course in year three and switch by year five

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It's not just my job, it's my friends and every renter I know, all at once. A basic income and serious public money for housing would help the most.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether we'd use AI to make things fairer or just faster. I use these tools every day, and they could cut agent fees for sellers by half. Whether that happens depends on who owns them, not on the tech.

headlineQuote: I use these tools every day, and they could cut agent fees for sellers by half.
portrait: Bianca sells flats for a small **online-first agency** and shares a flat with two friends.
She uses **AI tools daily** and is the office's go-to for systems, though an average closer.
Her steady worry is **housing costs**, which she campaigns on every Thursday.
As change speeds up, she moves toward **housing co-ops**, holding off on buying a flat.
With **ten years**, she feels hopeful and plans a second career in community housing.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her friends and every renter she knows would be hit at once.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** and serious **public money** for housing.
